outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no event has settled the Turing-completeness status of any elementary cellular automaton class other than Rule 110's (110, with 124, 137 and 193 by symmetry), which Cook proved Turing complete in 2004; the 2024–2026 events found are a 2025 re-verification of Rule 110 under a new formal ‘local universality’ definition, a June 2026 Zenodo claim by Nova Spivack of a ‘Cook-independent’ Turing-universality proof for Rule 110 that the same author narrowed to a finite NAND result in July 2026, a partial Lean library by the same author that calls itself not a Turing-universality theorem, and several discounted items about other properties; no 2024+ event addresses any of the other 87 classes.
problem_asks: The statement asks, for each of the 88 inequivalent elementary cellular automata (the 256 ECA rules identified under reflection and the 0/1 complement, Wolfram numbering; Rule 110 stands for the class {110, 124, 137, 193}), what its Turing-completeness status is: Turing complete (capable of universal computation), not Turing complete, or unknown. Parts: (a) the 88 classes taken one by one, since the statement says ‘all unique’ elementary cellular automata; (b) the status of each class as a matter of Turing completeness, meaning capacity for universal computation. The statement does not fix the initial-configuration convention, so it leaves open whether a rule counts as Turing complete when universality is allowed a periodic background pattern (as in Cook’s construction) or must hold from finite or blank initial configurations, and whether ‘universal’ means weak or strong universality. Those conventions are part of what the question asks and are not settled by the statement.

events.what_happened: Stephen Wolfram’s book A New Kind of Science (2002) claims Rule 110 is universal, a conjecture Wolfram had made in 1985, and includes an outline of the argument credited to Matthew Cook. Hughes (2012) cites NKS p. 707 for the claim that Wolfram and Cook claim to prove a (2,5) Turing machine universal via Rule 110. A search summary of Wolfram’s NKS notes (not opened in full) reports that rule 110, with 124, 137 and 193 as trivial reversals, is ‘the only clear immediate example’ among the 256 two-colour nearest-neighbour rules. The book is an announcement of an outline, not the complete argument; the complete argument is Cook (2004).
events.delivers: Claims, with an outline of the argument, that Rule 110 is universal (the class of 110, 124, 137, 193). The outline is not presented as a complete proof in the sources read.
events.remains: The complete argument (given by Cook 2004); every other ECA class.

checked_by.who: Dominic J. D. Hughes, author of arXiv:1208.6342
checked_by.qualification: Author of the 2012 arXiv critique; qualifications not established in the sources read.
checked_by.what_they_did: Found a critical gap in the Wolfram–Cook argument that a (2,5) Turing machine is universal via Rule 110, and offered a bridge (see hughes-2012).

events.doubts: The critique by Hughes (2012) concerns the (2,5) machine emulation that the book’s claim relies on; see hughes-2012 for what is and is not disputed.
events.direction: Toward universality for the Rule 110 class (the outline asserts it).

events.what_happened: Matthew Cook, ‘Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata’, Complex Systems 15(1), 1–40 (2004). Per a search snippet of the journal issue page (not opened; the page returned HTTP 500), DOI 10.25088/ComplexSystems.15.1.1. Wikipedia (opened) states that Cook proved Rule 110 with a particular repeating background pattern (fourteen cells wide, repeating every seven iterations) is Turing complete, by emulating cyclic tag systems, then 2-tag systems, then Turing machines, and that Cook first presented the proof at the CA98 conference in 1998, after which Wolfram Research obtained a court order excluding it from the published proceedings under an NDA dispute. The 2004 paper is the complete written argument found.
events.revisions: Only the journal version found. The NKS outline of 2002 is a separate event. The first public written date of the complete argument is not established: the journal year is used here, and an earlier manuscript circulation has not been ruled out.
events.delivers: Rule 110 is Turing complete, meaning capable of universal computation, under the periodic-background convention: infinite configurations with two different periodic patterns extending left and right, with initial structures arranged so they interact in an ordered way (Wikipedia). Covers the class of 110, 124, 137, 193. Per the sources read, it does not establish universality from finite or blank initial configurations, nor strong or intrinsic universality; Cook’s own distinction on this is reported in the 2012 FOM thread (search summary, not opened).
events.remains: Universality from finite or blank initial configurations (weak or strong); intrinsic universality; the status of the 87 other ECA classes.

checked_by.qualification: Researcher in cellular automata and computability; the affiliation (Laboratoire d’informatique fondamentale de Marseille) is from a search summary and was not checked on the page.
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a high-level re-proof of Rule 110 universality using particles and collisions, with a formal framework for Cook’s meta-structures (content from search summary; the PDF’s text was not readable by the tool).

checked_by.who: Jordan Cotler, Clément Hongler, Barbora Hudcová
checked_by.qualification: Authors of arXiv:2510.08342; qualifications not established in the sources read.
checked_by.what_they_did: Appendix re-checks Cook’s cyclic-tag construction against a formal local-simulation definition (read from the HTML version, first 100,000 characters of 256,465).

events.directly_checkable: The Rule 110 update rule can be checked by hand; the full emulation is a large space-time construction and is not directly checkable as a single object.
events.doubts: (1) Hughes (2012) reports a critical gap in the Wolfram–Cook argument for the (2,5) machine via Rule 110 and offers a bridge; this concerns the (2,5) emulation and is contested (see hughes-2012). (2) As reported in a search summary of the 2012 FOM thread, Cook says there is no proof of strong or intrinsic universality for Rule 110 or the machines it emulates; this limits the convention, not the weak result. (3) A search summary of Wolfram’s NKS notes says the proof was built over years with corrections and that some errors may remain; the notes page was not readable, so this is unverified.
events.direction: Toward universality for the Rule 110 class under the periodic-background convention. Wikipedia (opened) says Rule 110 is the only ECA for which Turing completeness has been directly proven, with proofs for similar rules as corollaries; Rule 124 is named as the horizontal reflection.
events.object: The Rule 110 space-time construction emulating cyclic tag systems, then 2-tag systems, then Turing machines, from a specified initial configuration with periodic backgrounds. Explicit construction, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Neary and Woods, ‘P-completeness of cellular automaton Rule 110’ (2006). Wikipedia (opened) states that Neary and Woods presented a construction replacing 2-tag systems with clockwise Turing machines, with polynomial rather than exponential overhead. A search summary says the paper shows that predicting t steps of Rule 110 is P-complete. The paper itself was not opened; the venue is not confirmed in the sources read.
events.delivers: Polynomial-time simulation of Turing machines by Rule 110, so Cook’s chain has polynomial overhead. A complexity refinement within the Rule 110 class; no new ECA class.
events.remains: The same parts as cook-2004-complex-systems; every other ECA class.
events.direction: Toward universality for the Rule 110 class (polynomial-time version).
events.object: A polynomial-time simulation of Turing machines by Rule 110 configurations; explicit construction, not a new object.

events.what_happened: Gaétan Richard, ‘Rule 110: Universality and Catenations’ (PDF on the author’s GREYC page; the PDF metadata gives a creation date of 21 January 2008; no venue found). A search summary says it gives a new high-level version of Cook’s proof using particles and collisions, with a formal framework for Cook’s meta-structures. The PDF was fetched but its text was not readable by the tool; only metadata was read.
events.revisions: None found. The date is from PDF metadata, not a venue.
events.delivers: A higher-level re-proof of Turing universality of Rule 110 by a different route; same class, same periodic-background restriction as Cook.
events.remains: The same parts as cook-2004-complex-systems; every other ECA class.
events.direction: Toward universality for the Rule 110 class.
events.object: The same universal Rule 110 construction as Cook’s, described at the level of particles and collisions; not a new object.

events.what_happened: Matthew Cook, ‘A Concrete View of Rule 110 Computation’, arXiv:0906.3248 (submitted 17 June 2009; EPTCS 1 (2009), pp. 31–55). The abstract (opened) describes an explicit compiler converting a Turing machine into a Rule 110 initial state, a general method for proving such constructions work, and a polynomial-time simulation of a Turing machine by a tag system, using the Neary–Woods methods.
events.delivers: An explicit, constructive compiler from Turing machines to Rule 110 initial states, extending the 2004 universality result. Same class; no new ECA class.
events.remains: The same parts as cook-2004-complex-systems; every other ECA class.
events.directly_checkable: The compiler is explicit, so a particular Turing machine’s Rule 110 initial state can be built and run; not done here.
events.direction: Toward universality for the Rule 110 class (constructive version).
events.object: An explicit compiler from a Turing machine to a Rule 110 initial state; the object is constructive.

events.what_happened: Dominic J. D. Hughes, ‘Is Wolfram and Cook’s (2,5) Turing machine really universal?’, arXiv:1208.6342 (submitted 31 August 2012). The arXiv listing calls it a 13-page draft that ‘languished untouched since 2007’. The abstract (opened) says Wolfram and Cook claim to prove a (2,5) Turing machine (2 states, 5 symbols) universal via Rule 110; the first part points out a critical gap, and the second part bridges the gap, ‘giving what appears to be the first proof of universality’. A September 2012 FOM mailing-list thread (read via search summaries, not opened) has Cook distinguish weak from strong universality, saying there is no proof or claim of strong or intrinsic universality for Rule 110 or the machines it emulates; Joe Shipman asks whether the machine is universal on ordinary blank tapes; Damien Woods agrees the draft does not address this and calls a positive or negative answer a breakthrough. Hughes wrote later that the (2,5) machine was never, and still has not been, proven weakly universal, and asked whether finishing the paper was worth the effort.
events.revisions: One version (v1) on arXiv. The draft was originally written in 2007.
events.delivers: Claims a bridged proof that the (2,5) Turing machine is weakly universal via Rule 110. Restricted to that one machine and to weak universality (infinite non-blank tape convention). Does not change any ECA class’s status, because Rule 110 is already settled.
events.remains: Strong universality of the (2,5) machine on blank tapes (open per the FOM exchange); the other ECA classes.

checked_by.who: Joe Shipman and Damien Woods (participants in the FOM mailing-list thread)
checked_by.qualification: Named participants; qualifications not verified in the sources read.
checked_by.what_they_did: Public commentary: Woods agrees the draft does not address blank-tape universality and says a positive or negative answer would be a breakthrough; Shipman frames the open question as universality on ordinary blank tape.

events.doubts: The author’s own 2012 FOM follow-up says the (2,5) machine was never proven weakly universal, and asks whether finishing the draft is worth the effort; this conflicts with the abstract’s claim of a first proof. The draft is unfinished per its arXiv listing. No independent verification of the bridging argument was found.
events.direction: Cuts against the Wolfram–Cook claimed proof (critical gap), then claims a repair toward universality of the (2,5) machine via Rule 110. Contested in the FOM exchange.
events.object: A specific 2-state, 5-symbol Turing machine emulated by Rule 110 via a ‘wrap construction’ (as described in a search summary of the FOM thread); an explicit construction.

events.what_happened: Pierre-Étienne Meunier, ‘Unraveling simplicity in elementary cellular automata’, arXiv:1406.5306 (submitted 20 June 2014; cs.CC). A communication-complexity classification of ECAs. Theorem 1.1 (read in the HTML version): ‘55 of the 88 non-isomorphic elementary cellular automata are not intrinsically universal.’ Section 4.1, ‘The last candidates to universality’, says ‘The status of the following 33 cellular automata remains open:’ and lists rules 3, 6, 9, 11, 14, 18, 22, 25, 26, 30, 33, 35, 37, 41, 43, 45, 54, 57, 58, 62, 73, 74, 106, 110, 122, 126, 134, 142, 146, 152, 154, 164 and 204. The introduction says Cook showed rule 110 ‘is capable of arbitrary Turing computation’. The section does not name the open property; it is inferred from Theorem 1.1 to be intrinsic universality.
events.delivers: Classifies 55 of the 88 ECA classes as not intrinsically universal, a stronger simulation notion than Turing universality. Says nothing directly about Turing completeness of any class. Its open list of 33 is for the intrinsic property and includes rule 110, which is Turing complete; it is not a Turing-completeness status.
events.remains: For intrinsic universality: the 33 listed rules (property inferred). For Turing completeness: the paper does not address the question.
events.doubts: The property named by the open list is not stated in section 4.1; reading it as Turing completeness would be wrong, since rule 110 appears on the list while known to be Turing complete.
events.direction: Negative for a different property (intrinsic universality) for 55 classes; open for 33 classes for that property. No statement on Turing completeness.

events.what_happened: Genaro J. Martínez, Andrew Adamatzky and Harold V. McIntosh, ‘Complete Characterization of Structure of Rule 54’, arXiv:1410.3096 (submitted 12 October 2014; journal reference Complex Systems 23(3), pp. 259–293, 2014). The abstract (opened) describes Rule 54’s gliders, glider guns and soliton-like interactions, and an abstract machine recognising regular expressions of gliders. The abstract reports no Turing-universality result for Rule 54. A search summary attributed to this paper two statements — that no one has implemented an equivalent Turing machine in Rule 54, and that Rule 54 is universal in the memory-augmented ECA classification. The abstract page contains neither, so those reports are not confirmed.
events.revisions: One version (v1) on arXiv; journal version in Complex Systems 2014.
events.delivers: Structural characterisation of Rule 54 (gliders as regular expressions). No Turing-completeness result in the abstract. Discounted for the question.
events.remains: The Turing-completeness status of Rule 54 (described as open in a 2020 lecture slide and a MathWorld snippet, neither opened).

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the published version.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; refereeing not examined. Publication is not a verification of universality.

events.direction: Neither; structural analysis of Rule 54 with no universality claim in the abstract.

events.what_happened: Jürgen Riedel and Hector Zenil, ‘Rule Primality, Minimal Generating Sets, Turing-Universality and Causal Decomposition in Elementary Cellular Automata’, arXiv:1802.08769 (submitted 24 February 2018). The abstract (opened) proves that Boolean compositions of ECA rules 51 and 118, and of rules 170, 15 and 118, can emulate ECA rule 110, making them Turing-universal coupled systems; builds a 4-colour Turing-universal cellular automaton carrying a Boolean composition of two and three ECA rules; and reports a candidate minimal set of 38 prime ECA rules that generate the other non-trivially symmetric ECA rules under Boolean composition. A listing (not opened) places the journal version in the Journal of Cellular Automata 13(5–6), 2018.
events.delivers: Turing universality of coupled systems built by Boolean composition of two or three ECA rules, via emulation of rule 110. Makes no single-rule Turing-universality claim in the abstract. Compositions are not single ECA rules, so the result does not bear on the 88 single-rule statuses.
events.remains: The single-rule status of the 88 classes; the composition results are outside the question as stated.
events.direction: Toward universality for compositions of ECA rules, not for single rules; discounted for scope.
events.object: An explicit Boolean composition of ECA rules 51 and 118 (and of 170, 15 and 118) that emulates rule 110.

events.what_happened: Jordan Cotler, Clément Hongler and Barbora Hudcová, ‘Self-replication and Computational Universality’, arXiv:2510.08342 (submitted 9 October 2025; one version, v1). The abstract (opened) constructs a cellular automaton that is Turing-universal but cannot sustain non-trivial self-replication. In the HTML version (first 100,000 of 256,465 characters read): Theorem 2.4 states that Rule 110 is locally universal with respect to an encoder–decoder pair with polynomial time complexity; Conjecture 3.1 (open) states that Rule 110 is in UniversalSelfReplicating; Appendix A.2 describes ‘the proof of local universality of Rule 110: a 2-state 3-neighbor 1D CA’ and notes it can simulate a universal Turing machine in polynomial time; Appendix B.1 says some elementary CAs ‘have been shown to be Turing-complete’, citing a reference. The abstract and sections read do not say whether the Turing-universal CA the paper constructs is elementary, one-dimensional or two-dimensional.
events.revisions: One version (v1), as listed on arXiv.
events.delivers: Re-establishes Rule 110 (a class settled by Cook 2004) as locally universal under a new formal definition with a polynomial-time encoder–decoder. Does not add any ECA class to the Turing-complete list. Restriction: this is local (encoder/decoder) universality, not the plain Turing-complete statement the problem uses.
events.remains: Membership of Rule 110 in UniversalSelfReplicating (Conjecture 3.1, open); the other 87 classes, which the sections read do not address; the identity of the paper’s own Turing-universal CA, not established from sections read.
events.direction: Confirms the direction for the Rule 110 class under a new definition. Leaves the ECA question otherwise unchanged.
events.object: A cellular automaton constructed in the paper that is Turing-universal but cannot sustain non-trivial self-replication (its dimension, state set and neighbourhood not established from sections read); also the Rule 110 encoder–decoder pair of Theorem 2.4.

events.what_happened: Zichao Wei, ‘On the Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Generalization in Neural Networks’, arXiv:2602.01651 (v1 submitted 2 February 2026; v2 revised 21 April 2026; cs.LG). The abstract (opened) proposes a neural cellular automaton architecture (SEAD), reports results on parity, addition and Rule 110, and names the Rule 110 result ‘learning a Turing-complete cellular automaton without trajectory divergence’. A search summary says the model is trained under supervision on known Rule 110 transition rules; the body was not read.
events.delivers: A learning result: a neural model that reproduces Rule 110 dynamics from known rules. No universality property is proved. ‘Turing-complete’ is the background description of the rule, not a result of the paper.
events.remains: All of the problem; the paper does not bear on the ECA classes’ status.
events.doubts: The phrase ‘learning a Turing-complete cellular automaton’ is not a universality result for any ECA class; treat as not bearing on the question.
events.direction: Neither; it learns an already universal rule.

events.what_happened: GitHub repository novaspivack/rule110-lean (‘The rule 110 Lean library’, Lean 4; 104 commits per the page). The README (read via the raw file, summarised) says it is ‘A Lean 4 formalization of Matthew Cook’s proof that Rule 110 is computationally universal’. Its top theorem is cook_operational_stage3_tm_microstep_readback, which the README calls ‘an operational partial result, not a Turing-universality theorem’, adding that ‘full unconditional Turing universality remains open’. It has five named ‘Cook bridge axioms’ (cook_cts_data_cones_origin_one_step_ax, cook_cts_eval_sim_at_data_cones_origin_step_degenerate, cook_cts_phased_post_decode_ax, cook_cts_tail_origin_ax, cook_cts_tail_origin_final_ax); the README says these are ‘mathematical facts proved by Cook (2004)’ and that they ‘have not yet proved in full Lean generality’. A separate finite result, rule110_center1_nand_functional_completeness, rests on the axiom boolean_nand_complete (Sheffer 1913). Commit 5509e9b (6 July 2026; committed by novaspivack and cursoragent, with trailer ‘Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>’) renames rule110_turing_universal_algebraic to rule110_center1_nand_functional_completeness, states the old name was misleading because its statement is ‘exactly finite two-input Boolean/NAND functional completeness’ and ‘not a Turing-universality result’, and says Rule 110’s Turing universality remains rule110_turing_universal_from_cook. Commit eb5a0e3 (25 May 2026) corrects the NAND attribution to Sheffer 1913.
events.revisions: Earliest commit visible on the first page of the history (34 commits) is 19 May 2026; the repository’s creation date and the rest of the history were not read. Later visible commits: 25 May 2026 (eb5a0e3), 30 May 2026 (adds a Martínez phases catalog), 6 July 2026 (5509e9b and one other rename).
events.delivers: A partial Lean formalisation of the microstep-level structure of Cook’s construction, conditional on the five axioms, plus a finite Lean theorem that with the centre cell fixed to 1 the rule is NAND on its neighbours. By the author’s own README it is not a Turing-universality theorem. For the ECA question it adds no class; it re-formalises Rule 110, which is already settled.
events.remains: The five Cook bridge axioms (not formalised in full generality, per the README); an unconditional Turing-universality formalisation (stated as remaining open in the README).

machine_checked.notes: Per the README, the top theorem compiles with zero sorry; five Cook bridge axioms and boolean_nand_complete are Lean axioms. I did not run the Lean build, so this is the author’s claim.

events.directly_checkable: The library source (Rule110.lean and the Rule110/ directory). Not run.
events.doubts: (1) The README calls the five axioms ‘proved by Cook (2004)’ while also saying they are not yet proved in full Lean generality; in Lean they are assumed, so the top theorem is conditional on them. (2) The GF(7) Zenodo record (spivack-gf7-2026) was presented at v4 as Turing universality; the repository rename in 5509e9b matches the later narrowing. (3) The commit trailers name Cursor as a co-author on at least one commit; the role of Cursor in the proofs is not stated (see ai).
events.direction: Toward Cook’s Turing-universality result, as a conditional formal reconstruction. The author says it is not a Turing-universality theorem.
events.object: A Lean-formalised ‘operational’ readback of a cyclic-tag-system compilation into Rule 110 microsteps, conditional on five axioms; and a Lean proof that with the centre cell fixed to 1 the rule is NAND on its two side cells (a finite Boolean result).
people: novaspivack (GitHub account; the author’s site novaspivack.com lists this repository, and the Zenodo deposits name Nova Spivack)

events.what_happened: Nova Spivack, ‘Deeper Consequences of Arithmetic Universality in the Standard Model’: Zenodo deposits with successive versions (records 20466125, published 20 May 2026 as v2; 20550101, v3 published 4 June 2026; 20682688, v6 published 13 June 2026). The abstracts (read via the Zenodo pages) claim the Standard Model generation orbit is ‘forced to evolve under Rule~110 — a Turing-complete binary cellular automaton’ and that principal results are ‘machine-certified in Lean 4’. The records do not cite Cook’s proof or claim any new universality result; they take Rule 110’s Turing completeness as given. A Zenodo catalogue (20573114, 6 June 2026) lists the programme’s 49 papers and a rule110-lean dependency.
events.revisions: v2 published 20 May 2026 (the earliest version found); v1 not located, so the first public date may be earlier. Later versions v3 (4 June), v6 (13 June); further versions exist.
events.delivers: Nothing on the ECA question. Uses Rule 110 as a physical substrate and presupposes its Turing completeness; adds no ECA result.
events.doubts: The physics claims are self-reported and not evaluated; they do not bear on the question.

events.what_happened: Nova Spivack, ‘Algebraic Characterization of Rule 110 over GF(7) and Cook-Independent Turing Universality’ (Zenodo record 20562119). The v4 record (published 5 June 2026) abstract, as read from the record page and a search summary: a degree-3 multilinear polynomial over GF(7) reproduces the eight Rule 110 transition values; with the centre cell fixed to 1 it reduces to NAND of the side cells; by Sheffer’s functional-completeness theorem the author concludes Rule 110 is Turing universal ‘via a Cook-independent algebraic route’; ‘All results are machine-certified in Lean 4 with zero sorry’, with one named axiom (nand_complete) capturing Sheffer’s result. The latest version read, v10 (published 6 July 2026; record 20562119/latest; title ‘Algebraic Characterization of Rule 110 over GF(7) and Finite NAND Functional Completeness’), states: ‘This is a finite Boolean result: it does not imply Turing universality’; that the result ‘is independent of Cook’s 2004 proof that Rule 110 is Turing universal’; and that ‘Cook’s route establishes Turing universality’. The record also links the result to a ‘Universal Generative Principle’ physics framework (Klein–Gordon substrate, lepton mass hierarchy), which was not evaluated.
events.revisions: v4 (5 June 2026) is the earliest version I could read; versions v1 to v3 were not located, so the first public date may be earlier. v10 (6 July 2026) is the latest read. Versions v5 to v9 not read. v4 title: ‘…and Cook-Independent Turing Universality’; v10 title: ‘…and Finite NAND Functional Completeness’.
events.delivers: At v4, the event as read claims Turing universality of Rule 110 by a route the author calls Cook-independent. At v10 the author says it establishes only finite Boolean NAND functional completeness for the centre-1 rule, and disclaims Turing universality. On either reading it adds nothing to the ECA question beyond Rule 110, which Cook settled.
events.remains: On v10’s own reading, Turing universality of Rule 110 is left to Cook’s 2004 proof, and the question of the other classes is untouched. The Turing step of v4 is not supported by the argument shown in the abstract.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (per the record; the Lean file is Rule110/AlgebraicUniversality.lean in novaspivack/rule110-lean, per commit 5509e9b)
machine_checked.notes: Author states ‘zero sorry’ in the abstract; one axiom nand_complete acknowledged. Not verified by me; the Lean build was not run, so this is the author’s claim.

events.directly_checkable: The eight-entry identity: I checked p(L,C,R) = C + R − CR − LCR against all eight Rule 110 entries by hand and it holds; it also holds over the integers, so the GF(7) choice is not needed for the identity. With C = 1 it gives 1 − LR, i.e. NAND(L,R) on {0,1}.
events.doubts: (1) The step from a NAND gate at one cell to Turing universality is not supported by the abstract: a single-cell gate does not by itself give computation over unbounded space-time; Cook’s construction does this by emulating cyclic tag systems. The author’s v10 concedes this. (2) The Lean certificate covers the author’s stated lemmas and the axiom nand_complete. (3) The Klein–Gordon and lepton-mass parts are unrelated speculation and were not evaluated. (4) Self-published; no peer review or independent engagement found.

withdrawn.what: Author’s scope concession, not a formal withdrawal: v10 (6 July 2026) retitles the work to finite NAND functional completeness and states it does not imply Turing universality. The v4 claim of ‘Cook-Independent Turing Universality’ is no longer asserted. The repository commit 5509e9b (6 July 2026) states the same narrowing.

events.direction: At v4: asserts Rule 110 is Turing universal, in the expected direction for the class, by a route the author calls Cook-independent. At v10: no Turing-universality claim; only a finite Boolean NAND completeness result.
events.object: A degree-3 multilinear polynomial over GF(7) matching the eight Rule 110 transition values; with the centre cell 1 it reduces to NAND(L,R). An explicit algebraic identity, not a computational construction.

events.what_happened: Tigran Nersissian, ‘Diagonal Bases and Diagonal Periods of Elementary Cellular Automata’, arXiv:2609.25078 (submitted 18 September 2026; nlin.CG, cs.FL cross-listed). The abstract (opened) says exactly 24 rules give universal binary bases (in every finite window and every modulus), that Rule 124 is among them, and gives a Rule 30 polynomial construction and a finite census of additive periods. ‘Universal’ here means basis universality in linear algebra, not computational universality.
events.delivers: Nothing on Turing completeness. Different property (basis universality); discounted for the question.
events.direction: Neither; a different property of the same rules.
events.object: A census of 24 rules whose diagonal translates form universal binary bases (a linear-algebra property); not a computational object.

disputes.summary: Credit for the Rule 110 universality proof: Wolfram conjectured it in 1985 and his book (2002) outlines it, and Cook produced the proof. Wikipedia credits Cook (2004). A non-disclosure dispute with Wolfram Research blocked publication of Cook’s CA98 presentation for several years (Wikipedia, opened). Not resolved here; recorded for the later pass.

Whether Wolfram and Cook established that the (2,5) Turing machine is universal via Rule 110. Hughes (2012) says there is a critical gap and offers a bridge; the FOM exchange and the author’s own later comment say weak universality of the (2,5) machine was not established, and blank-tape universality is open. Hughes’s abstract claims a first proof.

The author’s own documents disagree on whether the Rule 110 result is a Turing-universality result: the Zenodo GF(7) record at v4 says ‘Cook-Independent Turing Universality’; v10 (6 July 2026) says it ‘does not imply Turing universality’; the repository README says the Lean top theorem is ‘not a Turing-universality theorem’ and full unconditional universality ‘remains open’, while calling its five axioms ‘proved by Cook (2004)’.

summary: The sources show one ECA class with a settled Turing-completeness status: Rule 110 with 124, 137 and 193, proved by Cook (complete paper 2004; outline in Wolfram’s 2002 book), under a periodic-background convention. I found no source settling Turing completeness, or non-completeness, for any of the other 87 classes. Rule 54 is repeatedly described as suspected but unproven (Martínez et al. 2014 do not claim universality; the search summaries of a 2020 lecture slide and MathWorld say open, neither opened). The earliest work that touched the other classes is Meunier (2014): 55 of 88 are not intrinsically universal and 33 are open for that property, including rules 54 and 110. That is intrinsic universality, not Turing completeness, and the sections read do not name the property; reading it as Turing completeness would be wrong. Riedel and Zenil (2018) prove Turing universality of compositions of ECA rules, not single rules. For 2024 to 2026 the events are as follows. Cotler, Hongler and Hudcová (arXiv 2510.08342, 9 Oct 2025) prove Rule 110 locally universal under a formal encoder–decoder definition and leave Rule 110’s membership in UniversalSelfReplicating open (Conjecture 3.1); this re-verifies a settled class. Nova Spivack’s Zenodo record (v4, 5 June 2026) claimed Rule 110 is Turing universal via a GF(7) polynomial, NAND gate and Sheffer’s theorem, described as ‘Cook-independent’, with Lean certification assuming one axiom. The argument shown does not get from a single-cell NAND gate to Turing universality, which is the central gap; I checked the eight-entry identity by hand and it holds. The v10 record (6 July 2026) is retitled to finite NAND functional completeness and says it does not imply Turing universality, and the author’s GitHub Lean library (rule110-lean, commits from 19 May 2026) says it is an operational partial result conditional on five Cook-bridge axioms and that full unconditional universality remains open. Both are self-published with no external engagement found. The remaining 2026 items (Spivack’s Standard Model deposits, Nersissian’s basis-universality preprint, and Wei’s neural-network learning of Rule 110) do not bear on the question as stated. Close calls for the later pass: (a) whether the v4 GF(7) claim counts as an event about Rule 110, which it does, though it adds nothing to the class; (b) whether the v10 change is a withdrawal or a concession, recorded as a concession by the author; (c) whether Cotler et al.’s Theorem 2.4 is a new result, recorded as a re-verification under a new definition; (d) whether Hughes (2012) changes the status of Rule 110, recorded as bearing on the (2,5) machine and on the weak/strong convention only; (e) whether Meunier’s open list counts, recorded as a different property. AI: no system is credited with the mathematics in any event. Cursor (‘Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>’) is a named co-author on at least one commit of the rule110-lean repository, including the 6 July 2026 rename that touches the Lean file for the GF(7) claim. The commit body changes names and docstrings, and no author sentence says what Cursor did, so no ai.systems entry is recorded; ai.none_found is false for the two Spivack events that rest on that repository. The Zenodo pages, the README and the author’s site say nothing about AI use. I found no report of an AI system proving or disproving universality for any elementary cellular automaton (searches 8, 9, 19, 20, 21, 35, 38, 43).
competing_reading: (1) Against the sceptical reading of the GF(7) record: the v4 abstract asserts Turing universality of Rule 110 by an independent route and says all results are Lean-certified, so a reader could count it as a second, independent proof of the Rule 110 class; the record’s author later narrowed it, but the earlier version is still public and was never withdrawn. (2) For the rule110-lean repository, the README calls its five axioms ‘proved by Cook (2004)’ and describes them as ‘mathematical facts’, so a reader could treat them as established results and the library as a near-complete formalisation of Cook’s proof; the README itself says they are not yet proved in full Lean generality. (3) On the 2012 (2,5) machine: Hughes’s abstract claims a first proof of universality, which a reader could count as a 2012 event that changes the Rule 110 class’s status; the FOM exchange and the author’s own later comment deny that weak universality of the (2,5) machine was established. (4) On Meunier (2014): a reader might count the 33-rule open list as the open set for the problem, but the list is for intrinsic universality and includes rule 110, which is already Turing complete. (5) On the convention: if ‘Turing complete’ requires universality from finite or blank initial configurations, then Rule 110 itself would not count and the settled set would be empty; the statement does not fix this, so the count depends on the convention.
what_would_settle_it: (a) Cook (2004) read in full, to confirm the periodic-background statement and to see whether any blank-tape or strong-universality claim is made; (b) Hughes’s complete paper or a later note on the (2,5) machine’s weak and strong universality; (c) an external review or Lean-Zulip discussion of the v10 GF(7) record and of the five Cook-bridge axioms, and the full text of versions v1 to v9 of the Zenodo record to date the first public argument; (d) the full commit history of novaspivack/rule110-lean, to see what Cursor produced in the proofs and whether any axiom has since been discharged; (e) a per-class table of the 88 ECA classes from a survey or the Wolfram Atlas, and a 2024–2026 arXiv full-text search for ‘elementary cellular automaton’ with ‘universal’ or ‘Turing’ in nlin.CG and cs.FL monthly listings, which I did not fetch; (f) the full text of Cotler et al. (2025) to identify the Turing-universal CA they construct and whether it is elementary; (g) the Meunier (2014) text to confirm the property named in its open list.

dead_ends: Wikipedia List of unsolved problems: the ECA entry was not found in the first 100,000 of 294,882 characters fetched; the statement given to me is used as written.
No 2024–2026 event found for any ECA class other than the Rule 110 class (no new universality proof, no new non-universality proof).

No report found of an AI system proving or disproving universality of any ECA (searches 8, 9, 19, 20, 21, 35, 38, 43); the AI-related results were LifeGPT (2024), a transformer learning ECA rules (Burtsev 2024), AutomataGPT (2025), and a 2024 paper on LLM computational universality (arXiv 2410.03170, not about ECAs).
No Lean, Isabelle or Coq formalisation of Cook’s proof other than novaspivack/rule110-lean was found in searches 29 and 43; the Wolfram Cloud notebook (Hajek) does not formalise Cook’s proof.
Rule 54: no universality proof found; Martínez et al. (2014) abstract reports structure only; a Rule 54 'universal in ECAM' statement could not be confirmed on the abstract page.
Rule 37R (reversible): the 2022 Wolfram Community thread has no reply and no answer; no proof found.
Rules 137 and 193: only the symmetry argument ties them to Rule 110; no separate proof found.
Rule 52: a 2016 PeerJ preprint (search snippet) says rule 52 contains a universal Boolean operator but has not been shown computationally complete; PeerJ page returned HTTP 403, so not opened.
Rules 90 and 150 (linear): no Turing non-universality result found. Meunier (2014) rules out intrinsic universality for linear CAs (search snippet of the same paper); that is a different property.
Zenodo versions v1 to v3 of record 20562119 were not located; the Zenodo versions list showed only v4 on the cached page.
Physics Forums and Wolfram Community 2022 thread: a question only, no answer.
